cells.tense: A fair exchange is moving between you and someone else right now, and its weight is felt before it is counted.
cells.ask: Pick one exchange that's working — a split that came out even, a favor returned — and spend this week not tending it. No evening up, no improving, no pointing.
cells.core:
When you and someone settle something fairly, you feel it settle — the proportion lands before you've worked out why. This is what it looks like going well: a trade gets made, both sides feel it, and you can spot the fair ones across a room without pulling out a ledger. The recognition arrives first. The arithmetic, if it comes at all, is only confirming.

What that costs is that fair trades stay quiet. Nobody notices a scale that isn't tipping, so the finished ones tend to get tended anyway. That's the fault this week — you reaching back into something already settled. Pick one exchange that's done and leave your hands off it. No adjusting, no evening up. The form is finished. The question is whether you can walk past a finished thing.
cells.sheetLine: You feel a fair trade before you can add it up.
cells.verb: Giving and receiving fair share, without arithmetic
cells.place: The place in you that recognizes what matters before you can account for it

cells.tense: You are already reaching to settle the next exchange before the last one has finished being made.
cells.act: keep going without checking on anyone else
cells.ask: Before you give — time, help, money — wait a day. If it still seems right tomorrow, give it then. No asking, no checking, no tally. Just the wait.
cells.core:
You see what's owed before anyone says so, and you move to fix it — sometimes before the other person has noticed there's anything to fix. In its good form, this is quick, clean generosity: you give, they receive, the thing evens out. The speed, though, has outrun the exchange. Your hand is already moving while the other person is still choosing.

What's driving the hurry isn't generosity exactly. It's the fear of being the one left owing. So the ask is delay, not distance — one day between the impulse and the hand. That gap is where an exchange gets to arrive at its own pace instead of yours. You don't have to calculate anything. You just have to not go first, for once.
cells.sheetLine: You give before the other side has asked.
cells.verb: Giving and receiving fair share, without arithmetic
cells.place: The place in you that recognizes what matters before you can account for it

cells.tense: A fair exchange was offered, and the giving went through while the receiving stayed on the other side of the door.
cells.act: strike one thing from the list that does not serve
cells.ask: Take a task or worry you're carrying for someone else and cut it. Drop it from the list and don't put anything back in its place. Nothing needs saying.
cells.core:
There's a place in you that recognizes what counts before you can argue for it, and lately it has gone quiet. You see the imbalance — you just don't act on it. Something that should have been give-and-take became give only, and the part where something comes back was left standing outside.

The route out isn't more effort. It's subtraction. Sort what's yours from what isn't, and take one load off that doesn't belong to you. No announcement, no settling of accounts. Just one thing no longer carried. The recognition comes back once the load is light enough to hear itself.

cells.tense: The exchanges near you stay fair because you quietly keep them so, and your account of it is that you were only nearby.
cells.act: write both sides of it on one page and close the page
cells.ask: Take one situation between two people and set both readings down — fair to one, unfair to the other, both true. Write them side by side, shut the page, no verdict.
cells.core:
The fairness around you has a keeper, and that keeper's account is that they just happened to be standing there. You pick up the proportion before anyone explains it, and then it gets filed as if it drifted in unowned. The ones being kept level haven't bought the bystander story. They don't need to.

What you carry is usually two-sided: fair to one person, unfair to the other, both readings accurate. The pull is to settle it the moment you're asked and end the waiting. This week, keep both for a while instead — set them down next to each other and close the page. That's the work, and it doesn't need an audience to belong to you.
cells.sheetLine: You keep the fairness and call yourself a bystander.
